title: The Flight Simulator for Lawyers: Abdi Shayesteh and Jeanine Conley Daves on AI, Deliberate Practice, and the Future of Legal Training
author: Abdi Shayesteh · Jeanine Conley Daves

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Vendor market: Expanding maps require disciplined selection
st.an: The source does not contest disciplined AI adoption, and its benchmarking surveys could inform implementation. But its main substantive move is away from vendor-market mapping and product selection toward AI’s potential role in legal training and the decline of traditional apprenticeship.

st.t: Organisational adaptation: AI benefits require human control
st.an: The source contains only closing acknowledgements and no substantive claims about organisational adaptation, human control, legal training, employment, pricing or AI adoption. There is therefore insufficient evidence to determine its position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: The source accepts that weakened informal apprenticeship creates a legal-training gap and materially develops the cluster’s proposed response through a concrete, repeatable AI deposition simulator with configurable scenarios and feedback. It retains human mentorship while acknowledging that testing and uptake do not yet demonstrate improved performance.

st.an: The source accepts the value of contextual, task-specific legal software and materially extends the cluster by applying it to lawyer development: real-world simulated assignments paired with AI-assisted feedback. st.an: The source accepts that AI will reallocate routine junior work and materially extends the cluster by proposing realistic, repeatable simulation as a concrete capability-preservation and training redesign mechanism. It directly addresses the cluster’s apprenticeship risk, although its claimed learning, efficiency and client-value benefits are largely predictions and participant impressions rather than measured outcomes.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s shift from product announcements toward organisational readiness and realised adoption by emphasising lawyer training, institutional AI leadership and comparative maturity assessment. kp.k: Apprenticeship depends on uneven access to assignments and feedback
kp.d: Shayesteh describes his own development as dependent on access to a mentor and repeated, varied assignments with feedback. He argues that apprenticeship was already weakening before contemporary AI and that women and diverse lawyers disproportionately missed developmental opportunities. Separately, host Greg Lambert frames billable-hour pressures and remote work as undermining learning through observation.
qs: The more assignments you get, the more feedback you get, the better you become, the better your judgment skills develop.
And usually those were, unfortunately, diverse lawyers and female lawyers because the same people were getting the same deals over and over again.
But between the billable hour work and remote work, the osmosis training has kind of vanished.

kp.k: AI feedback supplements structured simulation and targeted human mentoring
kp.d: Shayesteh reports that AltaClaro began in 2016, expanded from five courses to over 60, and now serves over 100 Am Law 200 firms, correcting the introduction's figure of nearly 80. He says experimentation with immediate AI feedback began three years before the interview. He presents structured rubrics, rather than generic chatbot feedback, as a means of identifying learner strengths and gaps and allowing partners to target subsequent mentoring; objectivity and effectiveness are his claims.
qs: Today we have over 60 across a variety of practice areas, from corporate to litigation, real estate, lending, all this good stuff.
And we have now, actually you said 80, it’s over 100, Am Law 200 firms.
A few years ago, three years ago, we started experimenting with AI and giving immediate feedback on these simulated assignments
not random AI, not ChatGPT, but a very structured rubric framework where those things are consistent and they’re evaluating you in an objective way on how to improve.

kp.k: Deliberate practice develops judgment rather than automating advocacy
kp.d: The guests invoke K. Anders Ericsson's research on athletes and musicians to argue for active, focused practice with feedback rather than passive observation or CLE. Daves presents simulation as a way to develop strong litigators while AI takes on memos and research, explicitly retaining the need to check research. Shayesteh frames the objective as strengthening human judgment in interpersonal tasks, not replacing lawyers in those tasks.
qs: I think, Greg, it’s really the act of doing that really helps you to grow and develop.
hone in on those skills to really focus on what am I doing well, what am I not doing well given the feedback that you are provided.
AI is taking some of those other tasks in terms of memos, you know, research, even though you always have to check the research.
How can we leverage it for those things that hopefully AI will never replace and build the human muscle for judgment?

kp.k: DepoSim rehearses unpredictable interpersonal situations without live-case stakes
kp.d: Shayesteh describes a deposition simulator with AI witnesses, opposing counsel and a court reporter, including adjustable hostility and aggressiveness. Learners can practise for 10 minutes to six hours and receive feedback. The proposed mechanism is repeated exposure to difficult interactions that require spontaneous follow-up and adaptation, extending AltaClaro's earlier emphasis on written work products.
qs: So we built an AI witness, AI opposing counsel, AI court reporter, and guardrail framework leveraging the technology we had used with our benchmark tool.

And you can go in and toggle and say, give me a hostile witness, or you can say, give me an opposing counsel who is super aggressive as many times as you want, like a flight simulator and practice your deposition.
You go as little as 10 minutes or as long as six hours if you want.

kp.k: Pilot evidence concerns realism and willingness to reuse
kp.d: Shayesteh reports over 160 hours of testing by six firms, including Littler and K&L Gates; host Marlene Gebauer dates the pilot to the preceding February. Daves reports associate praise for realistic witness and opposing-counsel personalities and actionable feedback, including a '10 out of 10' assessment. Shayesteh reports that 94% of participants would use it again. These are reported pilot reactions and intended reuse, rather than reported measurements of subsequent legal performance.
qs: six firms put in over 160 hours of testing it and giving us feedback.
Great feedback in terms of it’s a 10 out of 10. Associates saying like this is really true to life in terms of the witnesses and the opposing counsel that you are dealing with.
94% of all participants said they would use it again for deposition practice.

kp.k: Learners control feedback sharing and isolate specific weaknesses
kp.d: Shayesteh says simulator experiences are for the learner, who may choose to share a transcript, feedback report or audio with a mentor. Feedback can direct subsequent practice toward particular skills, such as exhibit handling or following up on evasive answers. He presents this as a means of making mentoring more focused and efficient, rather than requiring mentors to begin with foundational instruction.
qs: But all of the experiences inside the simulator is just for the learner.
So if they wanted to, they could share the transcript, the feedback report, even the audio with a mentor.
And that was part of the feedback we received from the first go-round, the ability to keep going back in and selecting what you actually want to practice.

kp.k: Senior lawyers use simulation for warm-ups and collaborative teaching
kp.d: Shayesteh says the pilot revealed demand beyond the intended junior and mid-level audience: experienced litigators wanted warm-ups, especially for infrequent depositions or anticipated witness characteristics. He reports firms requesting deployment to all litigators, including partners. He also carries a firm chair's proposed use of live demonstrations and reports paired associate practice and group review, presenting simulation as complementary to human connection.
qs: as a result, the firms asked us to deploy it across all their litigators, including their partners and seniors, which was cool.
A chair of one of the law firms said, I want to use this. I want to pull up DepoSim in front of all my associates during a training session.
Some firms are saying, you associates pair up and divide the deposition amongst you and go practice against DepoSim afterwards, exchange your feedback notes, and then let’s come back.

kp.k: Simulation may replace developmental opportunities lost through task automation
kp.d: Daves anticipates firms moving document review and memos through AI, reducing activities through which junior lawyers traditionally mastered case materials. She predicts greater use of simulators to preserve critical-thinking development and accelerate early-career litigation skills, including deposition practice from day one rather than waiting several years for a live opportunity. These are expectations about future training, not demonstrated longitudinal outcomes.
qs: You used to have to be the master of the documents.
the document review and memos, like you said, all of that, a lot of firms will now move through AI.
I think that you definitely are going to see law firms using simulators and these types of synthetic environments for training going forward.
For them to have this opportunity to do it from day one is incredible.

kp.k: Equitable training requires access, flexibility and protected practice time
kp.d: Daves argues that broadly available simulation can reduce dependence on personal relationships for developmental opportunities and that scheduling flexibility helps lawyers with outside obligations. Lambert raises the distinct risk that extra-hours learning could disadvantage caregivers and others. Shayesteh responds with Littler's regular AltaClaro training arrangements: protected Friday time for an hour of video and a two-hour assignment, followed by a Monday live review, repeated the next month. This example concerns regular training programs, not an explicit DepoSim time-credit policy.
qs: I think it does create a more equitable playing ground in an environment that quite frequently it has been about sort of relationships
I think having the opportunity to actually be able to work it into your own schedule is something that is going to be more helpful than harmful.
Friday, they watch an hour of video, they do a two-hour assignment, and it’s blocked on their calendar, they turn it in. On Monday, it’s the live review session, and they get the report.

kp.k: Training investment is framed as reducing rework and write-offs
kp.d: Daves argues that independent practice reduces the need to involve expensive lawyers in preparing and conducting foundational training. Shayesteh argues that empathetic provision of safe practice reduces partner rework, unchargeable time and remedial explanations. He predicts that clients will favour firms producing better work more efficiently through training and tools. The discussion supplies a proposed economic mechanism, not quantified ROI or measured client migration.
qs: The time that it saves is critical.
firms are leading with empathy who are giving their associates the space and the tools to practice, to make mistakes, to get feedback so that they can be better prepared.
And you have to write that time off. You can’t charge the client.
And they’re going to go to those firms who invest in their associates and are creating better work product at a more efficient rate

kp.k: Medical analogy emphasizes feedback over years of experience
kp.d: In recounting Ericsson's book Peak, Shayesteh says radiologists five years out performed better at predictions than those 20 or 30 years out because recent training supplied outcome feedback that established practice lacked. He further says the findings transformed certification toward annual case-based prediction and feedback. This is his account of cross-domain research and its institutional implications, used to support feedback-based legal training; no study sample or numerical effect is supplied.
qs: They studied radiologists five years out versus 20, 30 years out in terms of their skills in predicting
It was the five-year-out.
They were getting feedback on the simulated assignments as well as real assignments.
And so this transformed the certification process for the radiology medicine, medical industry that they now have to every year go through case files and predict and get feedback on their prediction.

kp.k: Roadmap extends simulation to advocacy, negotiations and real cases
kp.d: Shayesteh says employment and commercial litigation cases are available and forecasts IP, antitrust and securities scenarios in the next few months. He identifies oral advocacy, cross-examination, meet-and-confer interactions and deal negotiation as subsequent applications. He says a Verbit partnership should enable real-case simulations by the following year with a security apparatus. Daves separately speculates about simulations of Supreme Court justice personalities. These are roadmap commitments and predictions, not descriptions of all current capabilities.
qs: We just launched the employment case. We have a commercial litigation case.
But the next few months, we’re going to have an IP case, an antitrust case, securities, all the key areas.
And then after that, we’re going to look at other simulation types in the trial process, oral advocacy, cross-examination.
especially in our partnership with Verbit, where, by next year, we’ll be able to simulate real cases. Obviously they’ll have a security apparatus for that and we’re prepared to do that.

kp.k: Standardized preparation could improve cost predictability and differentiation
kp.d: Shayesteh predicts that repeated practice and more consistent skill levels across firms will optimize the time required for real work, enable better analysis of what tasks should cost and lower client costs. His 'Intel inside' analogy presents training infrastructure as a quality signal clients might use to differentiate firms; he does not propose a specific billing-model change.
qs: I think one of the positive impacts is that we’re actually gonna have…  a better cost analysis of what things should cost.

if you have associates doing these reps, doing these reps, being better prepared, and you’ve equalized these skills across the firm, you’re now going to optimize the time it takes to do something like this in the real world.
it’s going to be more efficient, it’s going to be better, it’s going to cost you less.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI simulation is presented as a way to develop lawyers’ judgment through repeatable practice and structured feedback, rather than simply automate their work.
pts.d: Abdi Shayesteh says AltaClaro uses rubric-based AI feedback to identify strengths and gaps, enable targeted repetition, and make subsequent human mentoring more efficient. DepoSim extends this approach from written assignments to interactive deposition practice with simulated witnesses, opposing counsel and a court reporter. Jeanine Conley Daves says this supplies active skill development as AI takes over some memo, research and document-review tasks; she explicitly retains the need to check AI research. Both anticipate wider simulator-based training. Shayesteh also reports senior lawyers using simulations to warm up and firms using them for collaborative, in-person teaching—not just solitary training.

pts.k: The speakers predict more equitable training access, earlier skills development, lower training and rework costs, and competitive differentiation for investing firms.
pts.d: Conley Daves argues that broad access to simulation makes development less dependent on relationships with partners and lets juniors practice skills before receiving real deposition opportunities. She predicts rehearsal extending to Supreme Court arguments. Shayesteh argues that foundational simulation practice saves expensive lawyer time, reduces remedial work and write-offs, improves work-product efficiency, and will attract clients to firms investing in training and tools. He also predicts more consistent skills will improve estimates of what work should cost and reduce client costs. These are prospective benefits and economic arguments, not quantified outcome findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Evidence consists of vendor-reported adoption and pilot feedback, a participating firm leader’s experience, and deliberate-practice analogies.
pts.d: Shayesteh reports that AltaClaro serves over 100 Am Law 200 firms; this is platform-level adoption, not a count of DepoSim customers. He reports six firms conducting over 160 hours of prelaunch simulator testing and 94% of participants saying they would use it again. He describes firms subsequently requesting deployment to all litigators, including partners. Conley Daves reports Littler associates praising realism and giving a 10-out-of-10 response. These are usage, satisfaction and experience reports; the transcript supplies no participant denominator, controlled learning comparison, measured improvement in live legal performance, or quantified cost savings. Both speakers invoke Anders Ericsson’s deliberate-practice work; Shayesteh recounts a radiology example and discusses educational ideas associated with Salman Khan as supporting analogies, not legal-AI outcome studies. Shayesteh is the vendor CEO and Conley Daves represents a participating firm.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current deployment is distinguished from near-term product plans and undated predictions about broader professional change.
pts.d: In the transcript labelled 2026, Shayesteh dates AI-feedback experimentation to roughly three years earlier and describes DepoSim as recently launched. Employment and commercial litigation scenarios are already available; IP, antitrust and securities cases are planned within the next few months. Other simulation types—oral advocacy, cross-examination, meet-and-confer and deal negotiation—are later roadmap items without firm dates. Simulating real cases is projected for 'next year' (2027 relative to the document label), with a security apparatus and a Verbit partnership. Benefits depend on structured feedback, repeated targeted practice and firms allocating time for learning. Learners may share reports with mentors, but simulator experiences are described as private to the learner. Conley Daves’s predictions of wider training adoption and argument rehearsal have no specified completion date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include junior and experienced litigators, mentors, lawyers with unequal training access or scheduling constraints, law firms and their clients.
pts.d: Junior and mid-level associates are the initial training audience, gaining safe practice, feedback and earlier exposure to deposition skills. Partners and senior litigators also use the tool for preparation and demonstration. Mentors can concentrate on identified gaps rather than teach foundations from scratch. Conley Daves frames wider availability as reducing dependence on sponsorship relationships; Shayesteh’s account of uneven traditional assignments specifically mentions diverse and female lawyers. Conley Daves argues flexible scheduling helps people with outside obligations, while Shayesteh emphasizes protected training time and cites Littler’s scheduled AltaClaro coursework as an example, not a universal DepoSim policy. Firms may gain better-prepared lawyers and competitive advantage; clients are predicted to receive more efficient, less costly service. The discussion principally concerns law-firm training, especially large firms, not demonstrated public access-to-justice gains.
